title: When the Interior Turns
premise: After their mother's funeral, Lior Dunmore inherits not money but silence: a house full of unlabeled boxes, unsent letters, and a father who left decades ago and never explained why. When the childhood home in Marrow Bay goes up for auction, Lior returns to catalog it and discovers letters revealing that their mother chose duty over love, sending away the person she actually wanted. As the auction date closes in, Lior must decide whether to preserve the house as a monument to the lie or let it go — and whether to repeat their mother's choices or finally break them. The novel ends with Lior letting the house sell, reading the last letter aloud on the empty porch, and choosing the person they love over the inheritance of silence.
about_author: Lior Delacroix is the pen name of a former archivist who spent twelve years cataloging other people's unopened correspondence before turning to fiction. They write about inheritance, quiet betrayals, and the houses that keep our secrets.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Lior, POV, catalogs their mother's belongings after the funeral: labeled jars, an address book with pages torn out, a locked drawer they cannot open. The emotional beat is grief as bureaucracy — mourning conducted through lists. A realtor's call about the Marrow Bay house interrupts, forcing a decision Lior isn't ready to make.

chapters.title: Marrow Bay, Low Tide
chapters.summary: Lior drives to the coastal town they fled at nineteen, POV alternating briefly with memories of childhood. The house smells of salt and stopped clocks. An old neighbor, Ruth, recognizes them and says something unsettling: 'Your mother wrote to someone every week. Never said who.' The beat is dread disguised as nostalgia.

chapters.title: What the Auctioneer Knows
chapters.summary: Lior meets Dev, the auctioneer handling the sale — sharp, kind, and the person Lior once loved and abandoned for a career in the city. Their reunion is polite warfare. Dev mentions the house has drawn interest from a developer; time is short. The beat is attraction tangled with old guilt.

chapters.title: Letters, Unsent
chapters.summary: In the attic, Lior finds a tin of letters addressed to 'A.' — a name they don't recognize — spanning thirty years, all returned unopened. POV stays with Lior but the letters begin speaking in their mother's voice. The beat is vertigo: the parent Lior mourned was a stranger mid-story.

chapters.title: Ruth Remembers Wrong
chapters.summary: Lior interviews Ruth and other townsfolk, collecting contradictory versions of who 'A.' was — a sister? a lover? a child given up? Each account contradicts the last. The beat is the unreliability of belonging: everyone remembers the town differently, and none of them remember Lior kindly.

chapters.title: The Drawer Opens
chapters.summary: Lior finally forces the locked drawer and finds adoption papers — their own. 'A.' is Ada, the mother who raised them until age four before the Dunmores took her back through family pressure. The beat is betrayal refracted: Lior's whole life was the price of someone else's survival.

chapters.title: Duty, Illustrated
chapters.summary: Flashback chapters from the mother's letters trace her choice: poverty, a disapproving family, a marriage of logistics. Lior reads them aloud to Dev at night, and the two grow close again. The beat is tenderness under threat — Lior recognizing they are one bad compromise away from becoming their mother.

chapters.title: Ada
chapters.summary: Lior tracks down Ada, alive, elderly, living two towns over, and visits without announcing themselves. Ada knows instantly who they are. She doesn't forgive the Dunmores, but she gives Lior the missing half of the story — including a final letter their mother never sent. The beat is devastating, quiet recognition.

chapters.title: Going Once
chapters.summary: Auction day. The developer bids high; Dev runs the sale with professional composure while Lior watches their childhood sold lot by lot. At the climax, Lior stands and reads the unsent final letter aloud to the room — their mother's apology, addressed to Ada, copied in Lior's hand. The beat is public rupture, private release.

chapters.title: Everything Said
chapters.summary: Weeks later: the house belongs to strangers, Ada and Lior have begun an awkward, real relationship, and Lior has declined the promotion that would have taken them away again. On the empty porch at low tide, Lior mails one letter of their own — to Dev, asking for a beginning instead of an ending. The beat is chosen belonging over inherited silence.
